---
title: "What a p-value for interaction means"
format: html
---

This page explains what the p-value of an interaction term tests, and what it doesn't. It uses no results from this trial.

## It tests a difference between effects

The p-value of an arm × subgroup interaction tests one null hypothesis: **the arm effect is the same in every level of the subgroup**. A small p-value is evidence that the effects differ. It is not a test of whether the intervention works in any one subgroup.

A p-value measures how incompatible the observed test statistic is with a specified null hypothesis and model assumptions. It is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true, nor the probability that a result happened “by chance.” Here the null is about equal effects on the scale being tested.

Altman and Bland make the general point: to compare two estimates, test their difference directly; don't compare their separate p-values [@altman2003interaction].

## "Significant in one subgroup and not the other" is not evidence of a difference

A common mistake is to fit the model in each subgroup separately, find p < 0.05 in one and p > 0.05 in the other, and conclude the intervention works only in the first. Two estimates can be almost identical while one crosses 0.05 and the other doesn't, especially when the subgroups differ in size. Brookes and colleagues showed by simulation how often subgroup-specific tests produce this pattern when the true effect is the same in both groups, and that the interaction test is the right comparison [@brookes2004subgroup].

For example, two wholly invented estimates could both be an IRR of 0.80, with intervals of 0.65–0.98 and 0.55–1.16. One interval excludes 1 and the other includes it, yet the estimated effects are identical. The interaction test directly addresses whether the effects differ.

## It has low power

**Power** is the probability that a study's test detects a specified effect when that effect is present, under the assumptions used for the calculation. A trial sized to detect the overall effect has far less power to detect an interaction of the same size. In Brookes and colleagues' simulations, a trial with 80% power for the overall effect had only about 29% power for an interaction of that magnitude, and roughly four times the sample size was needed to match [@brookes2004subgroup]. In a pilot trial this matters even more: a large p-value for interaction is weak evidence that the effects are the same.

## It depends on the scale

As the [Interactions](methods_interactions.qmd) page explains, an interaction is measured on a scale. A test on the ratio scale (count models) and a test on the difference scale (mixed models) are answering different questions, and can disagree on the same data.

## Many tests

Each subgroup variable, outcome, population and visit adds tests. With several subgroups, several outcomes, two populations and an interaction p-value at every visit, some small p-values are expected by chance alone. Wang and colleagues' guidance on reporting subgroup analyses asks that the number of subgroup analyses be stated, that prespecified and post hoc analyses be distinguished, and that interaction tests rather than subgroup-specific tests be the basis for claims of different effects [@wang2007subgroup]. The retrospective [analysis plan](https://github.com/VagishHemmige/COHERO-RCT-analysis/blob/main/analysis-plan.md) currently treats the subgroup analyses as post hoc unless protocol documentation establishes otherwise; the code applies no multiplicity adjustment.

## Report the effects, not only the p-value

Because the interaction p-value says nothing about the size of the effect in each group, it's best reported alongside the effect within each subgroup level, with its confidence interval [@knol2012presenting]. [Effects behind an interaction](methods_stratified_effects.qmd) shows how to get those.


## Reading a subgroup result

Read the estimated effects and intervals first, then the interaction p-value. Ask what scale was tested, how precise each estimate is, and how many subgroup comparisons were examined. A wide interval and a large interaction p-value can leave substantial differences unresolved.

Start with [Altman and Bland's short Statistics Note](https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj.326.7382.219) [@altman2003interaction]. [Wang and colleagues](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMsr077003) provide a clinical-trial reporting checklist [@wang2007subgroup]; [Brookes and colleagues](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jclinepi.2003.08.009) give the simulation evidence on power [@brookes2004subgroup].
